characters: Ama: a nine-year-old Ghanaian girl in Primary 4, braided hair with bright yellow beads, wearing a coral-orange polo shirt, denim shorts and green canvas shoes.
Jayden: Ama’s ten-year-old cousin visiting Ghana from London, curly short hair, wearing a light blue t-shirt, beige cargo shorts and carrying a small digital camera.
Ranger Kweku: a friendly Kakum National Park guide in his thirties, wearing a forest-green ranger uniform and cap.

narrationPlan.voice: Warm, lively Ghanaian English storyteller (`Kore`) for Primary 3–4.
notes: Use phonetic hints for Ama and Kakum while keeping standard written spellings.

music: Optional rainforest birdsong and soft acoustic guitar, off by default.
culturalNotes: Highlights Kakum National Park in the Central Region and accurate UNESCO World Heritage vs Tentative List status.
reviewQuestions: Confirm that the watershed connection between Kakum River and Cape Coast water supply is clear for Primary 3–4.

pages.brief: Lush tropical rainforest entrance at Kakum National Park in morning sunlight. Ama (9, braided hair with yellow beads, coral-orange polo shirt, denim shorts) welcoming Jayden (10, light blue t-shirt, beige shorts, small camera) beside Ranger Kweku (forest-green uniform).
pages.narration: Bright, welcoming and proud. Emphasise "Welcome to our rainforest, Jayden!".

pages.brief: Wooden visitor pavilion at Kakum: Ranger Kweku gesturing toward a carved wooden trail map (no text or letters) while Ama and Jayden check their backpacks.
pages.narration: Clear, friendly authority for Ranger Kweku.

pages.brief: High wooden tree platform at Kakum: a narrow suspension bridge of wooden planks and high safety rope nets stretches between giant rainforest trees, with Ama and Jayden looking excited.
pages.narration: Build wonder and excitement on "Kakum Canopy Walkway".

pages.brief: Mid-bridge view on the Kakum Canopy Walkway: Jayden holding the side ropes while Ama smiles reassuringly beside him, surrounded by high green safety netting and sunlit rainforest canopy.
pages.narration: Gentle reassurance from Ama as Jayden finds his courage.

pages.brief: High wooden platform wrapped around a massive tree trunk: Jayden looking through his camera and Ama pointing as a hornbill and two mona monkeys move through fruiting canopy branches.
pages.narration: Hushed, excited whisper on the platform.

pages.brief: Ranger Kweku pointing downward from the tree platform toward the dense, undisturbed green rainforest floor and winding stream far below.
pages.narration: Thoughtful question from Jayden, clear explanation from Ranger Kweku.

pages.brief: Sunbeams filtering down to a crystal-clear forest stream flowing gently past giant buttress roots and ferns on the floor of Kakum rainforest.
pages.narration: Warm and emphatic on how the forest provides clean water for Cape Coast and nearby towns.

pages.brief: Shaded craft pavilion near the park entrance: smiling Ghanaian women and artisans displaying colourful woven baskets and carvings (no text signs) as visitors admire them.
pages.narration: Clear explanation of how ecotourism supports local livelihoods and conservation.

pages.brief: At the wooden trailhead bin, Jayden placing a clear plastic bottle into a neat wooden waste bin while Ama gives him a thumbs-up and Ranger Kweku smiles.
pages.narration: Proud, accurate distinction between inscribed World Heritage Sites and the Tentative List.

pages.brief: Warm afternoon light: Ama and Jayden smiling together as they look at a hornbill photo on the back of Jayden’s camera, with green rainforest hills in the background.
pages.narration: Warm, joyful ending. Gentle pause before "The end".

teacherGuide.overview: Set at Kakum National Park in the Central Region, this Primary 3–4 story introduces the Kakum Canopy Walkway, rainforest canopy habitats, watershed protection for Cape Coast, the economics and ethics of responsible ecotourism, and the accurate distinction between inscribed UNESCO World Heritage Sites and Ghana’s UNESCO Tentative List.
learningGoals: Explain what ecotourism is and state at least three responsible visitor rules in a national park.
Describe why the canopy walkway allows visitors to observe upper-canopy wildlife without destroying the forest floor.
Explain how Kakum’s rainforest protects the Kakum River watershed that supplies drinking water to Cape Coast.
Understand how tourism revenue and local jobs support conservation.

beforeReading: Locate the Central Region, Cape Coast, and Kakum National Park on a map of Ghana.
Ask learners: "If a cousin or friend from another country visited Ghana, what natural place would you be proud to show them, and how would you keep it clean?"
whileReading: Pause after page 4 to note the numbers: 7 bridges, 350 metres total length, up to 40 metres above the forest floor.
Pause after page 8 to trace where visitor money goes (park rangers, trail maintenance, local guides, village artisans).
afterReading: Have learners design a "Welcome to Kakum, Leave Only Footprints" poster listing three rules for visitors.
discussion: Why do more birds and monkeys live high in the rainforest canopy than on the dark forest floor?
How does protecting trees in Kakum help someone turning on a water tap in Cape Coast?
What is the difference between tourism that harms nature (littering, disturbing animals) and ecotourism that protects nature?
reflection: What natural place in your own community, a stream, grove, park, or beach, needs people to care for it the way rangers care for Kakum?

mathsExtension.task: The Kakum Canopy Walkway has 7 bridges with a total length of 350 metres. What is the average length of each bridge if they were equal?
If a school group of 10 children visits the walkway and each child’s ticket is 15 cedis, how much does the group pay in total toward park conservation?

support: Act out the four ecotourism rules from page 2 using simple hand gestures.
stretch: Write a postcard from Jayden to his school in London explaining three things he learned about Ghana’s rainforest.

culturalNotes: Kakum National Park was gazetted as a national park in 1992 and its Canopy Walkway opened in 1995 through collaboration between the Wildlife Division (Forestry Commission), the Ghana Heritage Conservation Trust, and Conservation International.

Accurate heritage note: Ghana’s inscribed UNESCO World Heritage Sites are the Forts and Castles (Volta, Greater Accra, Central and Western Regions, 1979) and the Asante Traditional Buildings (1980). Kakum National Park (Assin Attandanso Reserve) was placed on Ghana’s UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List in 2000.
localiseThis: Connect to the nearest protected forest reserve, wildlife sanctuary, waterfall, or river catchment in your region.

whatWeKnow: Tropical rainforest canopies house the majority of forest biodiversity because sunlight drives flowering and fruiting in the upper tree crowns.
Forested watersheds like Kakum regulate stream flow, filter sediment, and sustain municipal water supplies for Cape Coast and surrounding districts.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Canopy biologists are still cataloging hundreds of insect, orchid, and epiphyte species that live exclusively in the high crowns of West African upper-Guinean rainforests.

investigation.title: See How Forest Roots and Leaves Keep Water Clean
materials: Two cut plastic bottle funnels (or two small flowerpots with drainage holes)
Loose bare soil for Funnel A
Soil covered with dead leaves, grass roots, or moss for Funnel B
steps: Place bare loose soil in Funnel A over Cup A, and soil covered with a thick layer of leaves and roots in Funnel B over Cup B.
Pour the same amount of water slowly over both funnels to imitate rain falling on a bare hill versus a forested Kakum hill.
Compare how muddy or clear the water is in Cup A versus Cup B!
investigation.whatToNotice: The water filtering through the leaves and roots (Funnel B) comes out much clearer and flows more steadily, showing how forest cover protects rivers like the Kakum River!
investigation.safetyNote: Wash hands with soap and clean water after handling soil and leaves, and do not drink the test water.

factCheck.claim: The Kakum Canopy Walkway consists of 7 bridges spanning ~350 metres at heights up to 40 metres, and Kakum is on Ghana’s UNESCO Tentative List while protecting the Kakum River watershed.
factCheck.explanation: Kakum National Park (375 km²) protects the headwaters of the Kakum, Nemimi, and Nbuakosua rivers supplying Cape Coast; it is listed on the UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List (Ref. 1393, submitted 2000).
factCheck.reference: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Kakum National Park (Assin Attandanso Reserve) Tentative List Ref. 1393; Forestry Commission of Ghana (Wildlife Division).
